subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMCHITKA NUCLEAR TESTS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion under Standing Order 43 which I believe can be passed without debate. The matter is urgent and deals with the tremendous underground nuclear explosion which the United States plans to detonate at Amchitka Island in the Aleutians later this year. The best site is located near one of the main faults along the west coast of North America and there is great fear that both massive nuclear pollution and severe earthquakes could result from this nuclear underground testing. The view expressed in my motion has been stated by spokesmen for all parties in the House, and I believe it would be useful for this view to be formally recorded. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis):
That this House express its opposition to the proposed underground nuclear testing at Amchitka Island in the Aleutians and that this unanimous decision of the House of Commons be transmitted to the United States government through official channels.

speechtext: That this House criticizes the government for having neglected to institute the just society in Canada, as was promised, and which should have been a reality for a long time; by refusing to increase the basic income tax exemption for individuals, by refusing to repeal the 11 per cent tax on building materials and by failing to institute a guaranteed annual income scheme.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a great honour to propose the very important motion of censure before the House today. May I thank my colleagues for having entrusted me with such a delicate task which is also heavy with responsibilities.
During the debate, I intend to discuss certain matters, and several others will be dealt with by my colleagues. Then, together, we shall proceed so that by the end of the debate the government will be better informed thanks to our positive criticism and our suggestions for the pursuit of the objective to be reached, which is the establishment of a just society for all Canadians.
The motion of censure which I do not have to read again since you have done it with such brilliance, Sir, is vitally important.
The Speech from the Throne of the first session of the 28th parliament contained the following words:
My Ministers believe that much of the delay and difficulty in the handling of Parliamentary business during recent years could have been avoided or reduced by the improvement of Parliamentary rules and procedures. I
I entirely agree. We should devote less time to procedures of all kinds and act more quickly and efficiently by
Alleged. Non-Institution of Just Society avoiding the creation of useless committees. Sometimes, the government does not heed their recommendations, especially if they do not agree with its views.
In the 1968 Speech from the Throne, we could also read the following:
My Government is deeply and irrevocably committed to the objectives of a just society and a prosperous economy in a peaceful world.
Mr. Speaker, what is meant exactly by a just society? There must be agreement, not only on the meaning of the words, but also on the establishment and maintenance of this society. I would like, during the few minutes at my disposal, to indicate the different stages that a human being may go through during his lifetime if he is living in a society such as we know it.
In my view, in a just society, man and his rights must be the primary concern of government, in order to ensure that his needs, whatever they may be, are satisfied. The just society must, first of all, allow every Canadian to enjoy a maximum of freedom, happiness and well-being.
A just society is an ideal to which aspire civilized men. The government must, therefore, co-operate with individuals, with families and with the organizations of all sorts that men have created, in order to ensure better conditions for all, and not only for a privileged class.
Men got together to live in society for numerous reasons that I do not have the time to enumerate, but everybody knows that the main reason is the following: nobody is complete in himself. One person may be naturally gifted to perform a certain work, while another is suited for another type of work. The fact of living in society should enable each and everyone to satisfy his needs, from the cradle to the grave.
This objective has not yet been achieved for the Canadian people since two out of five Canadians are still living in dire poverty, in undeserved destitution, while Canada is chock-full of resources of all kinds. Large surpluses designed to satisfy the needs of Canadians fail to reach them, through a lack of financial means, of distribution, which prevents the advent of a just society for all.
In the Speech from the Throne of September 12, 1968, this could be read:
My Government believes that the objectives of a just society must always include the pursuit of a prosperous economy as well as the fair distribution of its proceeds. Poverty can be dealt with successfully and permanently only by continued and determined action in a variety of ways by all governments.
noon)
Therefore the government acknowledged its responsibility in this field. That is why we blame it for not having taken the necessary steps to correct an economic situation which is becoming more serious every day and which cannot be corrected automatically, even though the government may hope that time will settle everything, but I feel it will not.
People may say that it is not easy to eradicate poverty. In fact, it is impossible as Christ once said that there would always be poor among us. I agree that Christ

June 15, 1971
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society spoke in such terms, but by the same token he did not order our governments to administer the country in such a way that the poor would go on increasing in number so that the Gospel would not be given the lie.
Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to set forth the individual's rights only and to refuse to see his obligations also. We are generally all prone to talk mostly of our rights. That is human tendency. However, I must say that the individual may claim his rights if he has first recognized that he has obligations and responsibilities towards society and that he must fulfil them if he wishes society to do likewise towards him.
Except for some cases, citizens are fulfilling their duties towards society by contributions of all kinds, namely by working when it is possible to get employment in the industrial, business or professional fields, through services done to others.
I know it may not be to the advantage of a politician to speak of the individual's duties toward society and that it pays off much better, on the political level, to speak of his rights.
On the other hand I know that the duty of any responsible person occupying any function within society, at whatever level, is to recall on occasion that the individual, the family, corporations and labour unions all have rights, but that they also have obligations and duties they must carry out if law, order and justice are to prevail in the society within which they live.
It is also the state's obligation to see that the natural rights of man are guaranteed and respected throughout his life and to prevent the unfortunately all too frequent exploitation of man by his brother man; that is why there is so much malaise in our society, so many people wondering what tomorrow's society will be like. Is our Canadian society still a humane society where we love and help each other, or is it gradually turning into a wolfish society where we will devour each other?
The infant, from the moment he is conceived, has innate rights, among them that of life. This right is less and less respected and I find it strange that the government, through legislation, contributes to this feeling of contempt as concerns the right to live. How, then, can the state not be expected as a consequence to become permissive and allow all kinds of abuse against the person, when it is the state that leads the way.
The family, Mr. Speaker, is the living cell of our society, it has its own natural rights, and it is the duty of the state to see to it that it duly prospers so that each of its members can grow and develop in normal surroundings while getting the best that society can offer. These goods must be in sufficient quantity so that everyone is assured of an honest livelihood and this is not a fact yet.
In order to provide the Canadian family with the social benefits that can be derived from our economy, it must be granted a guaranteed annual income, something which most workers and farmers cannot achieve through the usual source of income, that is the salary of the worker or the net income derived by the farmer from his operations.

That is why I believe the government should immediately amend the legislation authorizing payment of family allowances to make the rates consistent with the cost of living and take into account the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, as the government recently did when he proposed an increase in postal rates.
I contend therefore that families are entitled to the allowances because human resources, the greatest wealth of the country, usually originate and develop within the family. Indeed, what would be the use of all our material wealth if there were no people to use it. For that reason,
I conclude that human resources are our greatest asset.
Considering that the Providence has given us all kinds of resources and that the people coming from families have been able through their work to transform them into a wide variety of useful products, it clearly follows that it is materially possible that family allowances be increased.
Consequently, what is materially possible and humanly desirable must be so financially. Money is only a sign of wealth and not wealth itself. There is therefore no reason why the signs should be rare when there is an abundance of things.
Strange things go on in our Canadian society. We talk of a just society. Yet, there are stricken families now in Canada where the father has either disappeared, died, been taken ill or laid off, and the mother must depend on social welfare. Most of those families, as I said before, already received some pension or other from the state, half of which, incidentally, is paid by the Canadian government, although the administration is provincial. That pension was not high enough to enable those families to live decently, yet, recently, that pension was reduced for all sorts of pretexts.
The family is often broken apart. In one case, the mother will have the allowance that she used to receive reduced because her unemployed son is living with her. If he goes to live elsewhere, the mother's allowance will not be decreased. How logical!
In some other cases, if the mother is good-hearted enough to look after her children herself, the criterion used to establish the amount of her pension will be different from that which is used for the care of the same child when he is referred by welfare to another family or to some institution. Curious sort of reasoning!
When the child is living within his family, the community gives less to help the mother support him. When the child is referred outside, the community gives more. So, this legislation promotes the destruction of the family, of the family spirit. The mother who does her duty to maintain her family in existence is punished by the community in that she receives less in assistance than she would if her family were broken up. That is why we have not yet achieved the just society, as far as the respect due to the family is concerned. It is the very base of our society and moreover, it is not a man-made institution.
As he becomes a member of society, the child acquires certain rights, including that of access to the education
June 15, 1971

level of his choice, according to the talents his Creator has given him. But God knows that in some areas of this country, this problem still exists and a great number of students are looking for summer employment in order to earn a few dollars to help their parents finance their education.
I agree that the government has made a little effort this year with the Opportunities for Youth program. I thank the government on behalf of the young people who will benefit from it but I very much regret that there will be too many who will be ready to return to their studies in September without having earned a cent. That is why I say, once again, that we have not yet achieved the just society.
Yet, there would be much work to do in our forests, to ensure the quick growth of the trees. And this work could, in a great many cases, be carried out by students during the summer months, which would make them very proud, beside the fact they would have earned money, to feel they have been useful to their country:
When the child has completed his studies and has become an adult with diplomas, he seeks to enter the labour force but he encounters all kinds of difficulties in securing a job or in getting into business. Yet, in a just society, the right to work should be adknowledged not only in words, but in fact.
We have today a disturbing unemployment rate likely to move us farther away from the just society. Can Canada afford to have 700,000 workers remain unproductive because they have no work? I know that it is a difficult problem to solve, partly so because of automation, science and modem production techniques, in any field whatever. That is labelled as progress.
A great many workers therefore are the victims of progress. And so it will be necessary to veer away from the ordinary in order that the progress of which we boast with reason become a factor of real prosperity for the Canadian worker in particular and for society in general.
Since progress enables Canadians to produce more from one year to the next-according to statistics-with a more and more limited participation from workers, it is up to Parliament to compel the government to use other formulas, to provide each Canadian, in a just society, with access to his country's resources.
This is why I suggest to the government to look into the possibility of reducing working hours, so as to enable a greater number of persons to contribute, through their work, to production, and to provide most Canadians with the opportunity of going to work daily, so that each worker might at last think with pride that his trade, his profession, his diplomas are useful, and that he is contributing to the development and processing of his country's resources.
Scientists claim that only three hours of work per day would be required for the production of everything required by mankind.
This is the wish so often expressed by many people with whom I talk. They do not want unemployment insurance, but employment insurance. Most of the unem-
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society
ployed do not seek welfare assistance but a job to earn their livelihood.
Since there will always be 24 hours in a day, there will always be some idle time and the government should take the necessary steps to see that this leisure time be organized in a practical way toward a richer society, a man-sized society where we shall live a better life.
After you have finished working, then comes the time for retirement. I think that after having worked for an average period of 40 years, people over 60 years of age could possibly expect from our modern and increasingly automated society a decent income instead of a life of poverty. Since older people find it more and more difficult to retain their jobs, let alone find a new one, it would be all the wiser to pay the old age security pension to every person over 60 and if the recipient is married, to pay the pension to his wife even if she is somewhat younger.
In a just society, people are entitled to security after having worked all their life especially since most of them have been unable to save anything because every cent has been squeezed out of them through taxation to pay back interests to those who control and exploit the credit of our nation.
Mr. Speaker, I wish-

speechtext:
I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I would also like to thank my hon. colleagues for their generosity. I will devote this precious time to remarks of real public interest and I am convinced that my constituents as well as the Canadian population generally will see the merits of my case.

Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society
I would also have liked to speak about the serious problem facing my region and which affects hundreds of workers in the city of Montmagny. Indeed everyone knows that the closing down of the Chemcell Ltd. plant on October 1, 1971 will greatly harm this region. If this plan is carried out it will be really an economic and social catastrophe for the area.
We live in an underprivileged region and again I urge the government to consider all those families who live in Montmagny, who have been living in that area for a number of years; they have relatives, friends and customs which should not be put aside. A number of the workers in that plant are no longer young, and it will be difficult to retrain them, to make miners out of them, when miners are already losing their jobs because some mines are closing down.
In short, I ask, in the name of the principle of a just society, that no effort be spared in Montmagny so that the families who have settled there, who have a home there, may be able to keep that home and to continue working in an environment that they love.
Mr. Speaker, the grounds on which is based the opposition motion which I have had the honour to move are numerous. I would very much have liked, in the course of this debate, to speak on the right to property which is sacred and innate to the individual. I would have liked also to speak on the dignity of work. I would have liked to say that it is a blessing and not a curse. I would have liked to develop all these topics which are of general interest so as to inform the population that people's representatives, if they recognize its rights, have also the courage to speak of their duties as well as of those of the citizens.
We are often accused of criticizing without ever making any suggestions. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have often made some in the House. During my speech, I made workable proposals which, if they were carried out, would really help solve many problems and make attainable the road to just society.
In conclusion, I would like to make a final suggestion. I would not want the ministers to judge me too severely but I would like to say this: To attain such an objective, we will have, in any case, to take the bull by the horns, and face the situation so that the masters of finance become the servants of society and not the government's masters. If the latter feels embarrassed in such a work, let it give its place to others and the job will be done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert)-we bear the same name-for referring once again to the just society flaunted at the beginning of this session, although there has not been too much said about it this afternoon. In fact, what we did have was a philosophical discourse on rights and responsibilities.
Some mild suggestions were brought forward, which I must say seemed somewhat strange to me. Never before
have we had such things in the Creditiste philosophy. What we heard this afternoon was at best a vague argument whereby each will receive according to his needs and produce according to his capacities. Is that the basis of the Creditiste philosophy? Indeed, I can find nothing else in the remarks of the hon. member for Bellechasse.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH JUST SOCIETY
speechtext: You will have to read my speech over.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH JUST SOCIETY
speechtext:
The hon. member did say each was to receive according to his needs. But on the other hand, how will each participate in the production?
Let us study this motion. We must keep in mind that on the occasion of the first debate we had this year, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) proposed a motion to the effect that the House deeply regretted that because of the indecision and failures of the cabinet, the just society was now a distant ideal.
Today the government is blamed for having neglected to bring about the just society it had promised. Then we are told how we should proceed. Unfortunately, not much was said about the increase in the basic personal income tax exemption. Perhaps the colleagues of the hon. member will mention that. After all, the motion has been moved by the hon. member for Bellechasse. And we did not hear anything about the abolition of the tax of 11 per cent on building materials, although it seems to me that it is rather difficult to tie this with the just society.
I would have been anxious to know the hon. member's opinion on the question of guaranteed annual income. His colleagues will no doubt be able to inform us or enlighten us on that subject.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH JUST SOCIETY
speechtext: We will encourage you!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH JUST SOCIETY
speechtext:
I would say "enlighten", really.
On the other hand, let us examine the hon. member's statement since the Standing Orders do not allow me to go back to the motion of censure presented in October.

However, Mr. Speaker, it will be interesting to see just how this debate develops and whether or not the hon. member for Bellechasse has made his budget speech at this time, considering the fact that we heard a plea with regard to his constituents. But I would challenge the hon. member and his colleagues to explain the validity within their movement of the philosophy he expressed in his speech, that in a just society it would be a case of to each according to his needs, with each producing according to his capabilities and desires. I do not know anyone in this chamber who would dare put forward that philosophy because it is a completely unworkable one in our form of economic organization, within our framework of government, and in fact in the development of our society. I do not think there is a society in the world that really

June 15, 1971

functions on that basis. I suppose that in the farthest reaches of the most idealistic communism there may be some who would say that should be the philosophy, but there is no country in the world at present which operates on that basis, simply because it is impossible.
We all know that phrase "a just society" was an electioneering slogan utilized solely for that purpose and hastily dropped afterwards. There is no more reference to it now on an official basis. Of course the government failed to institute a just society, because a just society means a different thing to each individual. It was an empty slogan used to captivate people at the time. I know that on the government side there will be at least 50 different versions of what is meant by it, just as there will be on this side.
In a legalistic sense is it the individual against the state or is it the right of the mass of society? What is a just society? Is it that a man has a right to work? A lot of people deny that philosophy and certainly the trade union movement denies what is said to be the doctrine of the right to work. I know that a lot of people say that in a just society a man has a right to work and to use his capabilities; he has a right to advance, to gain and to gather unto himself the reward of his labours subject to his sharing with society part of the excess in order to take care of the less fortunate. But to what degree? What is the degree to which a man is his brother's keeper? How far does that go in a just society? We all have different concepts of that principle.
The proposition was advanced by the hon. member for Bellechasse that in order to provide gainful employment for everyone the workload should be shared. In other words, the necessary hours of work should be reduced so that everybody would participate in the work available. But who would determine what should be the norm in order to share the work? Is this to be the result of a ukase of some government official? Are we to have a timetable directing that a man shall work four hours a day this week, three hours a day next week and so forth? I should like to have a detailed explanation from the hon. members who are making this proposition.
The hon. member advanced a further proposition to the effect that the old age security pension should now be payable at age 60. At one time there was an auction as to the amount and I suppose there could again be an auction among the political parties as to the quantum in order to gain the support of elderly people. The age for qualification was reduced from 70 to 65 last year. This proposal suggests that it be reduced to 60 and if the spouse of the entitled person is younger he or she could also qualify. This is an interesting bit of political favour seeking but I do not know how it would be financed. Perhaps it could be done by imposing another three or four points on personal and corporate income tax and another two or three points on federal sales tax. The amount of money required to take care of the additional people between the ages of 60 and 65 would be
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society
astronomical. Perhaps we will find out from the hon. members how they propose to pay for it. If they are cranking out the old Social Credit or Creditiste system of using the Bank of Canada, we can dismiss it out of hand because it becomes an empty gesture.
I heard the hon. member speak about the rights of property. In a just society I think there are rights of property, although some would deny it. I do not know where they get the idea that if one has a need one just takes. Yes, this is a straight program of liberation, of general national scrounging. Of course it will never be tolerated in a society where there is an elemental degree of law and order for the protection of the ordinary citizen. It would be rejected by all but a tiny minority of people in this country, so it can also be dismissed.
The rights of property go much further than just the protection of the sanctity or protection from depredation by others. In addition, there must be the right that property shall not be confiscated through taxation or eroded by runaway inflation. There are so many ways that property can be protected. Although the hon. member spoke about the rights of property he did not say too much about the obligations that go with the use of property, that one must not use it to harm another. Within that framework we can talk about pollution and using one's property with a complete disregard for one's neighbours.
I should like to go to the other aspects of this resolution in the limited time at my disposal. I should like to hear the members of the Ralliement Creditiste state what they believe should be the level of base exemption for income tax purposes. Perhaps on Friday night we will learn whether the government has chosen to use the general exemption or the principle of a tax credit. This has been argued back and forth before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Unfortunately members of the Ralliement Creditiste did not participate to any great extent in those discussions. It will be interesting this afternoon to hear their eleventh hour or almost one minute to midnight views on tax changes. I hope one of their members will explain what they want. Do they want a general exemption of $1,500 per individual taxpayer or do they want the tax credit? My party thinks the latter is a more equitable solution, particularly for those people in the lower income groups. There is no doubt that the general exemption granted in the past operates to the advantage of the higher income groups because of the progressive nature of the high rates at the margins.
I find the ideas of aid to the building industry and the establishment of a just society hard to reconcile. These parts of the motion are simply being added. I suppose one could take all sorts of things that could be included in a just society. We could go right to the very beginning, to 1963, when the sales tax was added to the whole range of building materials. It must be remembered that the sales tax had applied to about 50 per cent of building materials even prior to 1963. If one knows anything about the Excise Tax Act one will recall that old and famous
24171-6J

June 15, 1971
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society Schedule III in which indicated materials were not subject to the manufacturing tax. Yet this tax was extended to the whole range of materials by the Minister of Finance in 1963.
I would say that if one particular tax has worked to the disadvantage of the country as a whole, that tax is the additional sales tax on building materials. The government was particularly interested in increasing year after year the volume of construction, particularly in the field of low cost housing and so forth and so on; yet the mere addition of this tax represented an unfair burden, especially on lower income groups which were relying on lower cost housing.
May I say that the tax has also affected others. For instance, a syndicate of veterans groups in Edmonton, working with the Alberta Housing Corporation and CMHC, put up a very fine set of units for senior citizens. These were not limited to veterans. Because of the impact of taxes, the first to be met being the sales tax on building materials, costs were greatly increased. Strangely enough, an organization or establishment of that kind must carry its full burden of municipal and educational taxes. The net result is that the basic rent has been set at $75 per month for a single unit or, in other words, for an individual. Just imagine what could have been done for senior citizens if no sales tax on building materials had been charged and if no municipal taxes had been charged. It is true that the municipality gave the lot for $1 per year. Imagine what would have happened if municipal taxes had been reduced by one-half. After all, Mr. Speaker, the individual elderly person who must pay $75 per month for rent alone will have a really tough time. Without question, a person whose income is limited to the basic old age security payment plus the guaranteed income supplement will not be able to make ends meet in that type of unit. In this area the government should move to establish a more just society. We ought to consider our senior citizens who have no funds or savings of any kind and who have no family that still recognizes some responsibility for caring for aged parents.
If I may finish my remarks, it will be more than interesting to see what sort of system of guaranteed annual income is envisaged by the proposers of this motion. The premier of British Columbia has come up with a particular version of that idea. I recall that in 1968 the idea of a guaranteed annual income was talked about, shall we say, as a proposal of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). At that time the government said that this idea would cost billions of dollars and scared the electorate. Now it seems that the guaranteed annual income has become almost respectable; in some cases it has become reverently respectable. I want to hear what the proposers of the motion have to say about this.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH JUST SOCIETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) and his colleagues for placing this motion on the order paper in order that we may discuss it today. The motion is moved under a Standing Order which does
not permit the matter to come to a vote. Perhaps that is good, because I should hate to see the just society voted down. It has already been negated by the government in power. Some of us still hope that we may move in that direction, but it is not yet in sight.
In the Speech from the Throne which was read at the opening of the present session, the just society was referred to as a distant ideal. That was different from the language we heard during the election campaign of 1968. However, even though the government put in the mouth of the Governor General the expression that the just society is now a distant ideal, there were also these interesting words in the Speech from the Throne: "A society which is not inspired by love and compassion is not worthy of the name." I am afraid that that is what we have under the present government, a society which is not inspired by love and compassion. It is a society run by technocrats who have preconceived ideas of what is important and who seem unconcerned about the suffering experienced and endured by a great many of our people.
The motion as drawn is rather wide. One could spend his time talking about the basic income tax exemption level, about the 11 per cent tax on building materials, about the guaranteed annual income, or one could look at the earlier words of the motion and talk about the government's failure to institute the just society. That is what I should like to do, and I should like to be very precise. It is true that for some people in their retirement years things are better. Certainly a great many more older people enjoy a half decent retirement today than was the case 30 or 40 years ago. Yet for many of our older and retired people life is still very tough. The reason for that is their inadequate income, and even that inadequate income loses its value because of rising costs and high taxation.
If I were to extend my reference to the 42 cent increase in the basic old age pension that was brought in by the government last December, this could almost be a case of reopening a debate that was closed. However, I shall just mention that fact and suggest that that increase was an insult to our older people and it has not been forgotten. Even with the $80 basic pension and the $135 that some people receive as a combination of old age security and guaranteed income supplement, the position has been getting worse and worse since the changes that were made last December which, for the most part, came into effect on April 1. Rising costs, of course, are a major factor in the worsening of the position of our retired

It has always been my view, Sir, that old age pensions should be universal and that we should not worry about the wealthy receiving them because the income tax can take care of that. If it does not take care of it sufficiently, it should be adjusted so that it will. I have no intention of reneging on that position and saying that old age pensions per se should not be taxed. I do say, however, that people who have nothing else to live on but their old age security, guaranteed income supplement and perhaps some other small pension that they receive, should get tax relief either through raising the income taxation level to the point where they are not hit or through the provision of a tax credit. It does not make sense to talk about a guaranteed income supplement for the purpose of bringing the incomes of people up to a certain point through government action and for the government then to turn around and reduce that income below that level by means of taxation.
I repeat that I support the principle of old age pensions being universal and being subject to taxation so that those in the upper brackets will pay it back. However, I submit that through a process of income tax relief levels or income tax credits, we should ensure that our retired people who do not have anything else to live on but their old age security pension and guaranteed income supplement, or an amount at that level, will not have to pay income tax.
I hope we are not just talking into the air when we make this plea today, Tuesday, June 15. I think, Mr. Speaker, that I can complete my remarks before we rise at one o'clock. The other group I have in mind is our veterans, particularly the veterans who are recipients of the war veterans allowance. Legislation was passed this year that improved the disability pensions paid under the Pension Act and also improved the allowances paid under the War Veterans Allowance Act. When the announcement of those two changes was made last December 2, it was to the effect that there would be a 15 per cent increase in payments made under the War Veterans Allowance Act. The people affected by this-and 1 am referring particularly to the recipients of the war veterans allowance-are to be forgiven for presuming that their position would be improved by 15 per cent. By the time the legislation was passed and the government
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society introduced a few regulations under the act, it turned out that this was not the case.
The ceiling on the permissible level of income of war veterans allowance recipients was not raised by 15 per cent but by the same number of dollars that the allowance was increased. That was bad enough as a sort of a catch in the whole deal, but the most unkind and unjust cut of all was the regulation passed under the War Veterans Allowance Act which forced war veterans allowance recipients to apply for the guaranteed income supplement regardless of whether they wanted to do that. The government argued that since these veterans or their widows come under the ceilings set up under the War Veterans Allowance Act, namely $161 per month for a single veteran and $271 for a married veteran, it did not matter whether a veteran receives his money as old age security and guaranteed income supplement or as a war veterans allowance.
Apart from the fact that there is a psychological situation and these veterans feel that it is unfair to be pushed from their own legislation onto general welfare, there is this item about which I was talking a moment ago, namely income tax. To force these veterans to take the guaranteed income supplement instead of the war veterans allowance, even though they may end up with the same gross income, must be looked at in the light of the fact that old age security and guaranteed income supplement are taxable whereas the war veterans allowance is not. These people who were already hurt by the fact that they did not get a 15 per cent increase in their total income on a gross basis have also had that figure reduced by virtue of the application of income tax. We cannot, blame veterans and their widows, particularly war veterans allowance recipients, for feeling that the just society, if it ever existed, has passed them by.
I could go on with other details which we have gone over a number of times such as the unfairness to the widow of a veteran if the veteran dies more than a year after this change was made. If the veteran dies in the course of a year from April 1, 1971, the widow receives the married rate for one year, but if he dies after that she does not. There are quite a few other things of this sort. Despite the fact that I am allowed 20 minutes, I am pressing on so I can conclude my remarks before one o'clock and so that other members will have the opportunity to speak on the just society before six o'clock this afternoon.
These are the two matters with which I wanted to deal. I criticize the government. I deplore the fact that with all this talk about a just society and a society which would be inspired by love and compassion, the government has not acted in the interests of these two groups of Canadians. It has been most cruel towards our senior citizens and our veterans. As far as this government is concerned, it has let the just society pass these people by. In their name, I deplore it as strongly as I can.

Major C. H. Douglas was an economist and a professional engineer, not a nobody like the hon. member for Edmonton West. The fight between the two is not a struggle for cost-sharing but a battle raging around imposition of taxation. The controversy centers around the question of knowing who should have the power to grab whose money and how it should be done. This is the controversy. It does not pertain to the monetary system. The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) thinks this is funny, but he knows that I am right. Priority no, competition yes. This means that we continue to tax but that the provinces must do the same. This means two taxes instead of one, this means that the citizens of Quebec will be happier. They will say: At least the Prime Minister has given us the benefit of being taxed more. What an improvement!
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take more time, but the way things are I could go on all afternoon. My colleagues also have something to say.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the stability of the modern world depends on the stability of its currencies.
However, it is obvious that the value of money is unsteady, but always and directly tied up to the value of production. If we produce more for one dollar, it is obvious that our dollar is worth a lot more, while if we produce less, our dollar is worth less.
One must understand that the stability of our modern world is based on the stability of the currency, as far as the currency reflects the facts. It is very doubtful that all the miseries inflicted on the British people by bad kings, bad Parliaments, bad ministers and bad judges would equal those imputable to a bad currency.
The same thing could be said about Canada. When the currency goes well, Mr. Speaker, everything is in good shape, but when the currency goes wrong, everything goes the wrong way.
When I asked the President of the Treasury Board- who is in the House-for some extra help for my office on the sixth floor, I was told: We have no money, you are not entitled to any additional aid. However, there are unemployed, people looking for work but the government has no money for that.
But to pay expenses for trips outside and inside Canada, for trips everywhere, for setting up government and ministerial offices, for laying wall-to-wall carpets- not small carpets at $5.80 a yard but carpets so thick you almost need snow-shoes to walk on in ministerial offices- for all that there is money. However where it comes to those who need money, they discuss the matter like they did last Tuesday and conclude that none can be spared.
I urge the President of the Treasury Board to give us the help we need in order to perform our duties as members of Parliament, and we are entitled to get that help in Parliament.
The minister is looking surprised. Perhaps he was not present but at any rate he is advised to take steps to give us satisfaction.
Mr. Speaker, a sound currency, one which retains its stability for repayment of debts, its purchasing power, and the purchasing power of salaries, of savings, of pensions, is the key to economic freedom, progress and development.
The objective of a monetary policy is therefore to preserve the stability of the dollar and to bring about maximum production.
In fact, next to maintaining law and order that should be the government's prime responsibility. You can never preserve law and order in a country unless finances are made to serve human beings.
It is a known fact that the value of money is determined by the value of goods and services and not that money, as the hon. member for Edmonton West stated before dinner, is a monetary illusion. That tends to prove
[Mr. Caouette.l
June 15, 1971

that he is carrying a hat rack on his shoulders rather than his head.
Goods and services determine the value of money. Thus, we should strive to maintain a constant balance between the amount of money being created and the output of goods.
We must implement immediately a monetary policy based on the maintenance of a fixed level of domestic prices. To this end, the central Bank must exercise its exclusive privilege to issue money so as to maintain a constant level of prices. Issuing money under this principle would not amount to an original debt and would not bear any interest.
Private banks should be allowed to borrow and to invest instead of creating book money for their investments which tends to expand or to restrict the money supply and to alter the value of our currency.
It is unbelievable that governments, one after another, should have allowed private banks to create and issue millions of dollars of new money, without any obligation on their part to maintain the stability of the purchasing power.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, we advocate the financing of public capital and new interest-free credits underwrit-ter by the Bank of Canada or an agency connected with it, which would reduce pressures now exerted on the money market and reduce the rates of interest. Public works financing through interest-free loans would allow for a rapid development of this country's social equipment, according to the needs and while material and human resources exist.
Such interest-free financing would result in the lowering of prices and taxes which are now a burden for all classes of citizens, especially low-income or fixed-income groups such as pensioners. The financing of public capital through the creation of new credits issued by the Bank of Canada would also result in freeing huge amounts of private capital that are now tied up in federal, provincial or municipal bonds. Such capital would become available to private enterprise, which will not have to turn to foreign capital any more. In due time the Canadian people will thus be able to regain control over their economy, to please the members of the New Democratic Party who are so much in favour of the recovery of economic control by Canadians. This would lead to lower consumer prices, a drop in the cost of living and the end of inflation.
The ultimate effect would be the improved condition of the people as a whole, which should be a target for all governments throughout the world, including that of Canada. If the Canadian government is unable to strive for that goal, I shall repeat what my colleague, the hon. member for Bellechasse, said at the beginning of his remarks: Let him step aside we are ready to do the job for him.

Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-Si. George's-Sl. Barbel:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to commend the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for introducing
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society
this very important motion and would like to commend also the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for making the plea on behalf of the veterans and the aged of the country.
The section of the motion to which I wish to direct special attention concerns the Liberal government's failure to come to grips with the problem of ensuring a minimum standard of living for all Canadians, including the working poor. For many people, this involves the introduction of some form of guaranteed annual income. In fact, many of the provinces are actively considering a guaranteed annual income scheme, as anyone who is reading the reports from Victoria will know. This subject has been on the front pages of the newspapers for the past few days.
First of all, let me define what I mean when I speak of a guaranteed annual income. The term refers to that family of proposals that have in common the aim of supplementing incomes in an attempt to raise and keep all incomes above a poverty line. Basically, the guaranteed income would place a floor of minimum income security under every Canadian so that all citizens would be assured of the basic necessities of life, whether or not jobs can be found for them.
There have been two occasions in the last six months when the Liberal government has broached the topic of a guaranteed annual income. In both cases, their discussions of the topic have been noted more for inconsistent reasoning and misleading arguments than for the intelligent appraisal that Canadians have had every reason to expect after the fanfare with which the Liberal government embarked on its so-called just society policy and its war on poverty. The two specific instances to which I refer are, first, the white paper on income security and, second, the proposed amendment to the Canada Assistance Plan to allow individual provinces to institute their own guaranteed income plans, as suggested last week at the welfare ministers conference. In each case, the Liberal government has shown a complete lack of responsible leadership and intelligent appraisal of how best to tackle the issues.
First of all, let us consider the white paper on income security. This was prepared under the direction of Deputy Minister Joseph Willard and took two years to research. Much was hoped from this study. Canadians expected the paper to include the announcement of a broad new social policy for the country. However, the white paper turned out to be a document that is utterly contradictory in the jumbled "social philosophy" of sorts that emerges from different pages. The attempt was made to present a philosophy which would appease at one and the same time both those who favour economic growth and no major redistribution of income and those who would like to see a guaranteed annual income and a more equitable standard of living for all.
The white paper avoids any discussion of the redistribution of the national wealth and talks only of the redistribution of existing income security payments. No attempt is made to rationalize the present patchwork quilt of income support programs; yet, current social

June 15, 1971
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society welfare measures are merely an accumulation of ad hoc responses to particular situations, and therefore provide widely disparate levels of financial support to persons in similar financial circumstances across the country.
The white paper poses the guaranteed annual income alternative in ridiculously naive terms. In chapter 6 there is this declaration:
The many defects that are apparent In the existing programs lead to a basic question. Why not do away with all these programs and introduce in their place one over-all guaranteed income program to provide all persons in poverty with a basic minimum income?
It then proceeds to show how difficult it would be to eliminate most existing programs, such as unemployment insurance, workmen's compensation and the Canada Pension Plan. Most advocates of a guaranteed minimum income propose such a plan as a replacement for schemes of social assistance only, and would leave social insurance programs intact. Social insurance programs are intended to prevent people from falling into poverty: a guaranteed minimum income would help out those already in a condition of poverty.
The argument for a guaranteed annual income is that it is a superior alternative to income support programs, those which help people in poverty, and not an alternative to income protection programs, those which keep people from falling into poverty. The great difficulty with income support programs now is that they do not pay enough and are therefore self-defeating. They alleviate hardship but they do not make the poor less poor, leaving poverty to breed more poverty. The claim made for the guaranteed annual income is that if the income floor is set high enough to ensure an adequate minimum, the vicious circle of poverty can be broken, giving supportive social services and rehabilitative programs a chance to succeed. Current income support programs simply perpetuate poverty; the guaranteed annual income looks to its eradication.
The white paper does not recognize this point, nor does it even make the argument. It talks about the need for greater emphasis on anti-poverty measures; but it ends up by proposing higher family allowances for low-income families and more money for the needy aged, which will still leave most recipients who are below the poverty line where they are-below the poverty line.
Another disappointing aspect of the white paper's approach to the guaranteed annual income is its discussion of work incentives. Incentive to work is cited as "the major criticism" of the guaranteed annual income approach, and further study and investigation is called for to find out what effects such a program would have on the incentive to work and save. This is an inexcusable oversight. Why did the white paper not evaluate how work incentives operate in guaranteed minimum income schemes in other countries and include an evaluation of the New Jersey experiment? Canada does not need to break new ground here because the information is already available. Furthermore, social workers state that there is not enough clinical evidence to support fears of a

loss of work incentive in a guaranteed annual income system. The vast majority of low income earners want to work and get ahead; thousands already work even now when they could do better on welfare. The few who refuse to work will either be tolerable deadweights or else they can be ruled ineligible for guaranteed annual income assistance, just as is done now in some welfare programs.
Secondly, most guaranteed annual income type proposals have incorporated into their schemes work incentives far superior to the present situation. Currently, "disincentives" are built into existing welfare programs, as individuals lose from their welfare cheque or subsidy any money earned or saved; therefore, they are encouraged not to work to supplement their meagre welfare payments and to break the poverty and welfare cycle. A guaranteed annual income proposal, then, provides more adequate work incentives than do the government schemes, although the white paper erroneously implies the opposite to be true.
Another hurdle to acceptance of the guaranteed annual income, states the white paper, is the problem of administering the program. This is a strange argument. One wonders whether the administrative task would be significantly different from that involved in administering the guaranteed income supplement and the proposed family income security program, the payments under each of which will be income-related. The white paper expects that family income security program would be related to the income tax system, as the guaranteed annual supplement is at present.
A guaranteed income scheme could also be related to the tax system. Therefore, it is unlikely that a guaranteed annual income could impose an additional burdensome administration problem. In fact, rather than increase the administrative burden, a guaranteed annual income might actually rationalize the existing government bureaucracies by tying more closely the operations of the income tax system and the welfare system.
Ignored also in the white paper's discussion of costs are estimates of the social and economic costs of poverty. On this subject, the National Council of Welfare has stated clearly the case that the alleviation of poverty through such measures as a guaranteed annual income may be cheaper than the costs we presently accept for coping with the problems originating from the condition of poverty.
It would be easy for me to continue for some time documenting the inadequacies of the government's discussion of a guaranteed annual income in the white paper. To say the least, it was very disappointing. Canadians expected a factual discussion on the guaranteed annual income, and instead received only an apologist's rationalizations for failure to take a positive, intelligent stand on the issue.
The second occasion for the Liberal government to broach the subject of a guaranteed annual income came at the welfare ministers' conference last week. There, the federal Liberals put forward a plan to amend the Canada Assistance Plan so that the federal government would
June 15, 1971

provide 50 per cent of the costs borne by the provinces in programs employing an income test, a measure which would allow provinces to embark on a guaranteed annual income plan with the federal government paying half the costs. What happened, all of a sudden, to the federal government's objection in November, 1970, to such schemes? Have they changed their minds about the overall cost of a guaranteed annual income being prohibitive?
In its White Paper on Income Security, the Liberal government rejected a guaranteed annual income on the basis that it was too expensive and that Canadians could not afford it at present. The government now has contradicted itself by offering to share with the provinces in instituting such a scheme.

There is another problem-how national standards could be maintained in the future if each of the provinces were to embark on a different guaranteed income scheme or, more importantly, refused to take up the federal offer to inaugurate its own guaranteed annual income. Furthermore, the implementation of such an amendment to the Canada Assistance Plan would only exacerbate the present situation in which there are wide variations in the provincial standards of social welfare schemes already instituted under the Canada Assistance Plan.
There is a wide range in provincial assistance available under the Canada Assistance Plan right across the country. The federal proposal will do nothing to close this gap. More l kely, the gap will increase as the more well-to-do provinces forge ahead with guaranteed income schemes while the poorer ones fall even further behind. Provincial differences in terms of dollar grants are matched by differences in the form of assistance available. This raises the question of "portability". The federal government has stated in its working paper "Income Security and Social Services" that because Canadians are now so mobile and move so frequently from one province to another, "It is important to the people involved that their income security benefits be portable", and, "It is important for this reason too that income security measures be reasonably uniform across the country." Individual provincial guaranteed income schemes negate this statement of federal philosophy. Portability is a definite problem arising from the government's new proposal.
Once again, I have not exhausted the inadequacies of the government's most recent proposals in the social security field. I cannot spend longer on the subject in the time allotted. I think I have demonstrated that the federal government's involvement in the income support field has been nothing more than a series of contradictions plus rationalizations for its failures to take leadership

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must join my colleagues of the Ralliement creditiste in censuring this Liberal government for having failed to establish the just society in Canada, as promised during the last general elections, in 1968. There is no need to study at length the present administration to discover the almost total failure of this government, for which publicity and trips abroad are more important than a sound and efficient administration of our country, Canada.
To censure the government is no fun. However, we must do it, in an attempt to awaken it if at all still possible-which I doubt-before the situation deteriorates again.
To realize a just society, a government must get. going, resort to short-term and long-term policies likely to allow each citizen to develop to the fullest and to enjoy freedom and security, while participating thoroughly in the economic life of the country, being no longer a marginal element as most Canadiens are now by reason of the lethargy of the present government.
At the present time we are not facing a lack of productivity in the Canadian economy, but rather an insufficient use of the available resources, and above all, a waste of labour. The government so-called anti-inflationary measures-as pointed out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his statements, as you will recall, were meant to reduce the total demand of the Canadian people whereas the economy could have easily met that demand.
However, what we need at the present time is an increased demand since our economy does not produce to its full capacity. And when it does produce, the production is not distributed for lack of purchasing power. Instead of following the policy advocated by us. The government has restricted the demand, and an unacceptable rate of unemployment has resulted.
According to Mr. Havilland, an economist of the Economic Council, the government policy has resulted in a $3 billion loss, while Le Machiniste, a well-known magazine, puts it at $4 billion. Mr. Firestone of Ottawa University, has estimated at over $2 billion the loss of 200,000 new jobs. Anyway, even if economists disagree on the amount of the loss, they all agree that the government has failed and is responsible for a loss of several million and even billion dollars.
More and more Canadians are depending directly on the government for their livelihood. Imagine, for instance, that in April 1971, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics published an official report which showed that over 152,000 people were unemployed for more than seven months, a record figure. The government must certainly be blamed for its complete failure.
The present economic stagnation is a direct result of the government's attitude for whom power means more studies, more inquiries, more white papers, more statements of senseless policies, more useless trips, instead of

June 15, 1971
Alleged Non-Institution of Just Society
some action designed to make each individual participate more fully in the economic life of his country.
Mr. Speaker, one must admit that poverty has increased in Canada. The number of poor people has increased. The number of unemployed people has reached appalling proportions. There are more than 800,000 of them.
Under the present administration, the indebtedness of Canadians has now reached incredible peaks: $13.4 billion. Under the present administration, the indebtedness of provincial and municipal governments has become the most serious problem in Canada, with debts totalling more than $38 billion, not counting interest paid to financiers.
As a result, it must also be recognized that national unity can only crumble, as is demonstrated by seven useless Federal-Provincial Conferences on the Constitution. Will the Constitution give food to the thousands of Canadians who are deprived of a minimum income to live on?
Mr. Speaker, even if we gave every Canadian a new Constitution, it would not solve their problem, it would not give them a guaranteed minimum income, it would not eliminate poverty in this country bursting with wealth.
Young students with their pockets full of diplomas are unemployed. This again is another sample of the results obtained with a Liberal administration. And that is only part of the sad record of our Prime Minister's administration.
Is that the just society promised by the Prime Minister? Is that the just society promised in 1968 to win votes? Is that the promised land? If that is it and if the government leaders cannot do their job, then let them move aside and we shall do it for them. If they recoil from tackling high finance, let them move aside and we shall do it for them. The federal government's first responsability is to provide a fair distribution of the nation's wealth-and let us not forget it-of the nation's production, across the country, and also to ensure equality of opportunity for all Canadians.
This is our challenge. I suggest that the government by means of the appropriate economic and monetary measures could control inflation and unemployment provided they stop being the perfect servant and slave to high finance. But to achieve this, our travelling Prime Minister-our carrier-pigeon-should at least understand that administering Canada means staying in Canada. One cannot administer the country from abroad, between two ski meets or two cocktails, accompanied by 42 newsmen whose expenses are all paid.
In Quebec, for instance, there are more than 600,000 persons on welfare. Is that what you call a just society? To this number can be added about 20 per cent of those who work but whose standard of living is only slightly over the poverty line. Is that the just society? This is what we are experiencing in the constituency of Lotbiniere, in Victoriaville, Warwick, Arthabasca and Princeville.
But why? Because we have a government controlled by finance which refuses to come to grips with the problem. All these people are the first to be affected in our ridings. They are the people who elected me to Parliament to say these things to the government, to make it see the light if it is still possible. All those people are the first to be affected when the cost of living goes up, because they have to spend most of their income, if not all of it, for food, clothes and shelter, which are essential to life.
If they are working, workers, farmers and others are probably not members of a union so they cannot fight effectively for salary increases as other union workers are doing. If they receive social welfare allowances, these are not adjusted to match increases in the cost of living. They are solely adjusted to their budget deficit. So the poverty level rises and the gap widens between the wealthy and the poor.
Mr. Speaker, one of the first things to do-and this is urgent-is to increase the basic personal income tax exemption. The government refuses to do so and we are blaming it for that today.
Then the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials should be abolished; it is inflationary and gives rise to an increase in the cost of housing and this prevents workers and the poorer people from owning their homes. The government refuses to repeal this tax. It says, through the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), that it is a difficult but necessary tax. It also says: Pull in your belt! Pull in one's belt for whose benefit? Not for Canada but for high finance. Today we blame the government for not having abolished that tax.
We must have a guaranteed annual income scheme. That is another solution. For over 30 years, the Credi-tistes have asked that a monetary system be established which would give to every Canadian, whatever his mother-tongue, his race, his culture, whatever the provisions of the Constitution, a minimum guaranteed income, taking onto account the production capabilities of the country, which are enormous. The government refuses to do it and resorts to an orgy of publicity in promising a just society. This is pure abstraction, Mr. Speaker!
We are blaming the government today for refusing to take action in this field.
On the whole, we have to adopt constructive measures, change our philosophy, stop discouraging personal initiatives. Instead of adopting restrictive, discouraging policies, why not take incentives to promote and support initiative on the part of the individual as well as of private enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, those are constructive suggestions to bring people to really participate in the economic life of Canada. This is not the policy of the present government. The present government through our carrier-pigeon Prime Minister visits foreign countries, praises-I should say gives away-our natural resources, imploring people

June 15, 1971

to give us financial permission to develop our own country.
At the same time, Canadians are being refused, not only the possibility of taking part in the economic progress of Canada, but their share of this production made by the machine rather than by them, since they are unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, if this government is unable to achieve a just society, if it cannot discharge its duties, its commitments, if all it can do is travel and organize useless federal-provincial constitutional conferences, let it move over and we shall do the job.
Suppression of poverty is a collective responsibility. Let us not forget that poverty generates poverty, and that the poor, the dependents of government, the unemployed no longer accept to be deprived of the essential and that modern mass media invite them to live the good life even though they are deprived of the basic necessities.
The disorders experienced in our Canadian cities are due to the existence of poverty in the midst of affluence rather than to ideologies or constitutions.
In Quebec, Mr. Speaker, some 600,000 individuals are included among the social welfare recipients whose family income varies between $1,500 and $2,000 per year, that is from $35 to $45 per week. They are the ones who live in the slums of our cities, on lands which they have toiled to clear up, generation after generation. Today, with its dairy policy, its policies on wheat and agriculture generally, the government discourages them and reduces them to utter destitution, while depriving them of a guaranteed minimum income. My colleagues who represent those unfortunate areas in our towns as well as in the country know that the government gorges itself on publicity with its just society, but ignores the fate of those people.
And when the children of those individuals, living in the Saint-Henri district in Montreal or in slums Lot-biniere or elsewhere on land which their forefathers have toiled to clear up-from which they are banished by the government-see the situation, they revolt. And, as my hon. colleague from Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), the leader of the Social Credit, said, we cannot accept their violent methods but we cannot blame them either since that is their only resort in a society which refuses to open its doors to them.
This government could say, as they do in Quebec: We spend five billion dollars on education annually. But why? To teach them to become educated unemployed? That they might realize their hardships even more? If at least that were the case, we could perhaps change something; but today education has become a welfare institution: it encourages the young to study a long time because there is no work for them. Why not spend as much money to create jobs as is invested in education?
Education is a wonderful thing, Mr. Speaker, provided it truly reaches the population and it really serves the interests of the individual to enable him to attain self-fulfillment.
In conclusion, small wage earners...
